You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

RNA binding proteins could regulate transcription through modulating RNA polymerase II involved transcriptional condensates with the aid of nascent RNA. However, whether this mechanism also contributes to tumorigenesis is still unknown. Here, we show the RBP AKAP95 is required for MLL rearranged leukemogenesis. Phase separation and RNA binding properties of AKAP95 modulate Pol II recruitment into condensates at genome-wide target sites. AKAP95 interact with MLL1 translocated fragment and their partial co-condensation leads to stronger AKAP95 binding towards MLL-AF9 target genes. Loss of AKAP95 significantly downregulates expression of MLL-AF9 targets and impairs MLL-AF9 driven leukemogenesis. AKAP95 is not essential for normal and regenerative hematopoiesis, rendering it an ideal target for leukemia therapeutics. As an endeavor for modifying condensates, we design a peptide JD-PI95 bridging AKAP95 to protein quality surveillance component HSP70. The peptide successfully impairs AKAP95 phase separation, attenuates gene transcription and inhibits MLLr leukemia cells proliferation. Our work demonstrates an important role of RBP condensates in tumorigenesis through regulation of transcription and a new method to perturb specific condensates for tumor inhibition.

---

## Introduction

Phase-separation involved transcriptional machinery assembly provides exciting insights to explain many puzzles in eukaryotic transcription regulation. Transcriptional condensates, initiated through the multivalent interaction among the intrinsic disordered regions (IDRs) of transcription factors, coactivators, mediators, chromatin remodelers and RNA polymerase II (Pol II), control several steps of gene activation, including preinitiation complex formation, transcription pausing and elongation, super-enhancer assembly, and mRNA splicing and processing1. Meanwhile, chromatin and newly synthesized RNAs modulate transcriptional condensate formation. Chromatin acts as a scaffold recruiting multivalent transcription-related molecules to trigger the formation of transcriptional condensates2. The yield of nascent RNAs determines the formation or dissolution of transcriptional condensates, working as feedback for transcription activation3.

RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) could bind to nascent RNAs, making them particularly important in studying how transcriptional condensates are modulated by other factors. Many pieces of evidence hint that RBPs and transcription factors, or Pol II, are engaged in the same condensates to regulate transcription. For example, RMB25 had much overlapped genomic binding with YY1, and facilitated the latter’s role in transcription activation4. WDR43 binding to 7SK RNA was intertwined with Pol II pause release, suggesting multiple biomolecular interactions occurring at mesoscale5. PSPC1 is a paradigm of how RBPs and RNA synergistically facilitate Pol II condensation and promote transcription in mouse embryonic stem cells6. However, whether RBPs modulation of transcriptional condensate formation is an underlying mechanism for tumorigenesis is still unknown.

Aberrant protein phase separation could be the potential cause for many cancers. Oncogenic proteins, ENL mutants, EWS-FLI1, and NUP98-HOXA9, acquired phase separation for persistent transcription activation to allow tumor cells rapid proliferation7–9. EML4-ALK fusion protein forming condensate in cytoplasm activated JAK-STAT pathway, leading to the transition of lung adenosquamous cell carcinoma from adenomatous to squamous pathologies10,11. On the other hand, emerging understanding about the molecular basis for these oncogenic condensates provides new opportunities to treat cancer. High-throughput screening of drugs identified LY2835219, which effectively dissolved EWS-FLI1 condensates and rescued EWS-FLI1-induced aberrant gene expression12. A peptide (FIP4) targeting FOXM1-IDR1 disrupted FOXM1 liquid-liquid phase separation, reduced breast tumor growth and metastasis13. Although condensate-modifying therapeutics is at its infancy, it is a promising avenue for treating condensate-driven diseases14.

We previously reported that an RBP, AKAP95, regulates pre-mRNA splicing15,16. Besides scaffolding RBPs, AKAP95 also interacted with many transcription/chromatin-associated proteins (Pol II, MLL2, DPY30, HDAC3)16–18. AKAP95 protein has a phase-separation property, which mediates its splicing activity and pro-oncogenic function. It is still unclear if and how AKAP95 regulates tumorigenesis through transcription, and how its phase separation property might be targeted for tumor control.

In this study, we found that AKAP95 was overexpressed in MLL rearranged (MLLr) leukemia compared to other types of leukemia. It is well known that oncogenic transcription underlies MLLr leukemogenesis19. We found a two-layer mechanism of transcription regulation by AKAP95 in cells. Phase separation and RNA binding properties of AKAP95 modulate Pol II recruitment into the transcriptional condensates at genome-wide target sites. AKAP95 interaction with MLL1 translocated fragment and their partial co-condensation enhanced AKAP95 binding with MLL-AF9 target genes, resulting in higher dependence of the MLLr leukemia-specific transcriptome on AKAP95. We also took advantage of host cell heat shock proteins in safeguarding protein homeostasis, designed a molecular tool to target AKAP95 phase separation, and tested its therapeutic function in inhibiting MLLr leukemia cell proliferation.

---

## Results

AKAP95 is essential for MLLr leukemogenesis
Through analyzing the MLL-fusion proteins interactome20, we found AKAP95 is one hit with 4 different MLL-fusion proteins (MLL-AF9, MLL-EEN, MLL-ENL, MLL-GAS7). This enticed us to check whether it plays an important role in MLLr leukemia. Firstly, we referred to the transcriptome of MLLr and non-MLL rearranged (non-MLLr) leukemias in different cohorts21–23. The mRNA level of AKPA95 was significantly upregulated in both MLLr acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) compared to the non-MLLr leukemias (Fig. 1a, b). AKAP95 expression was also higher in MLLr leukemia cells than the normal hemopoiesis stem cells (HSC) (Fig. 1c). We confirmed this result by quantitative PCR analysis of 16 primary AML patient bone marrow samples (MLLr, n = 5; non-MLLr, n = 11), and western blot analysis of several leukemia cell lines (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Fig. 1a, b). Moreover, both the previous mouse MLL-AF9 leukemia model24 and our own experiment showed that Akap95 was upregulated in Lin− bone marrow cells transduced by MLL-AF9 lentiviral vector compared to the counterpart (Fig. 1e). These data suggest that AKAP95 may play an important role in MLLr leukemia.

To address this question, we knocked down AKAP95 in different leukemia cell lines by shRNA lentiviral vectors. The result showed that only MLLr leukemia cell lines THP-1 (MLL-AF9), Molm13 (MLL-AF9) and MV411 (MLL-AFF1) were impaired in cell growth, but not the non-MLLr K562 (BCR-ABL) and HL-60 (TP53−/−) cells (Fig. 1f and Supplementary Fig. 1c). CRISPR score was below zero and negatively correlated with AKAP95 expression in AML cell lines in the DepMap dataset (Supplementary Fig. 1d). These data indicate that AKAP95 is critical for MLLr leukemia cells.

Using our previously established Akap95−/− mouse15, we investigated whether Akap95 is important for MLL-AF9-driven leukemogenesis. We transformed Lin− bone marrow from wildtype (WT) and Akap95−/− mice with MLL-AF9-IRES-GFP or MLL-AF9-IRES-RFP retroviral vector. Both types of cells had the similar transduction rate (Supplementary Fig. 2a). Then, we injected them into conditioned recipient mice through the tail vein. The recipients with WT cells transplantation succumbed to leukemia significantly faster than the recipients with Akap95−/− cells transplantation (WT median survival: 51 days; KO median survival: 93 days; P=0.0007) (Fig. 2a). When bone marrow harvest from the moribund recipients were subjected to Wright-Giemsa staining, WT bone marrow showed a more undifferentiated phenotype than Akap95−/− bone marrow (Fig. 2b). Immunostaining also showed that more myeloid progenitor cells (GFP+Lin−ckit+Mac1+Gr1+)25 existed in WT bone marrow (Fig. 2c). As a surrogate for assessing myeloid transformation, colony formation activity of transformed Akap95−/− cells was greatly reduced in the serial replating assay. Akap95−/− cells formed less compact and smaller colonies with the appearance of differentiated neutrophils/macrophages (Fig. 2d, e). We repeated the colony formation assay with sorted RFP positive cells and obtained a similar result (Supplementary Fig. 2b). For the colonies grown out in the third plating, we transferred them into liquid culture and harvested the cells for a western blot to check MLL-AF9 expression. WT and Akap95−/− transformed cells had a similar amount of MLL-AF9 expressed (Supplementary Fig. 2c). These results indicate that Akap95 is critical for efficient leukemogenesis driven by MLL-AF9.

From the primary leukemic bone marrow, we harvested the LGMP population (Lin−GFP+cKit+CD34+CD16/32+)24 (Supplementary Fig. 2d) and transplanted them into secondary recipients. The disease latency was greatly shortened, but WT leukemia cells still had stronger potency to cause recipients death (WT median survival: 25.5 days; KO median survival: 28 days; P=0.0022) (Fig. 2f), and to form colonies in serial replating (Fig. 2g).

We have previously shown that Akap95 is dispensable for homeostatic hematopoiesis15, but it remains unknown if it is important for hematopoietic reconstitution. We carried out competitive transplantation assays by transplanting CD45.2-marked WT or Akap95−/− bone marrow cells with CD45.1 bone marrow cells at a 1:1 ratio (Supplementary Fig. 3a). Mice receiving the Akap95−/− cells showed similar bone marrow, spleen, and periphery blood chimerism in all lineages as WT cells (Supplementary Fig. 3b–d). Together, all these data suggest that AKAP95 is required for efficient MLLr leukemogenesis, but not for normal hematopoiesis under either homeostatic or regenerative conditions.

Loss of Akap95 impairs MLL-AF9-induced transcriptome
We performed RNA-seq for the MLL-AF9 lentiviral vector transduced WT and Akap95−/− bone marrow cells 48 h post-infection. Totally, 674 genes' mRNA levels showed significant changes between WT and KO cells, with 377 genes upregulated and 295 genes downregulated (|log fold change|>0.58) (Fig. 2h, Supplementary Data 1). Gene ontology analysis showed that the molecular functions of downregulated genes were mainly associated with transcription regulation, while upregulated ones were specified in cell adhesion (Supplementary Fig. 4a). Moreover, the targets of HOXA9, MEIS1, and MYC were preferentially enriched in genes downregulated in the KO cells (Supplementary Fig. 4b). We confirmed the downregulation of several well-established MLL-AF9 targets and upregulation of myeloid cell differentiation marker genes (Itgam, Cd14) in Akap95−/− pre-leukemia cells by quantitative PCR (Fig. 2i). Metagene analysis showed that active transcription markers (H3K27Ac and H3K4Me3) were enriched more in WT than in Akap95−/− bone marrow cells (Supplementary Fig. 5a). To be specific, several well-established MLL-AF9 target (Meis1, Pbx3, and Cpeb2) loci had more H3K27ac modification in WT cells, while Itgam and Cd14 loci had a little more H3K4me3 modification in KO cells (Supplementary Fig. 5b), supporting the phenotypic difference.

AKAP95 interacts with MLL1 translocated fragment mainly through the IDR
To investigate the endogenous AKAP95 condensates in cells, we established the endogenous Flag-mEGFP-AKAP95 knock-in Hela (Hela KI) cells by CRISPR/Cas9 technique (Supplementary Fig. 6a–c). Both of the two positive cell clones showed discrete foci of endogenous AKAP95 in the nucleus. FRAP assay showed a fast recovery of the fluorescent signals (T1/2 = 4.12 ± 1.31 s) in the AKAP95 condensate after bleaching (Fig. 3a). To confirm the interaction of AKAP95 and MLL-fusion protein, we carried out two different assays, Co-IP and imaging method. Endogenous AKAP95 were immunoprecipitated together with overexpressed flag-HA-MLL1T (MLL1 translocated fragment) in 293T cells (Fig. 3b). When mcherry-MLL1T were expressed in Hela KI cells, AKAP95 condensates had partial co-localization signals with mcherry-MLL1T (Fig. 3c). To dissect the binding moiety of AKAP95, we made a series of constructs expressing individual regions of AKAP95 (aa1–100, aa101–390, aa391–550, aa551–692) according to the prediction of disordered region (Fig. 3d). Co-transfection of GFP-fused individual fragments with mcherry-MLL1T showed that aa101–390 (IDR1), but not the other fragments, co-localized with MLL1T and formed large aggregates in the nucleus. Replacing the previously reported six Tyrosine residues in aa101–210 with Serine (PS-mutant) abolished the co-condensation (Fig. 3e). We speculated that AKAP95 IDR1 interacts with largely disordered MLL1T (Supplementary Fig. 6d), somewhat similar to how transcription activation domain (also disordered) interacts with IDRs of many co-activator26. AKAP95 IDR1 had similar rates of negative and positive charged residues as MLL1T, while its net charge per residues was negative, matching the positive net charge per residues of MLL1T (Supplementary Fig. 6e, f). The assembly of AKAP95 and MLL1T into co-condensates may be the molecular basis for AKAP95’s critical involvement in MLLr leukemogenesis.

AKAP95 binds to the genome prevalently and contributes to gene transcription
To investigate AKAP95 function in transcription regulation, we carried out anti-flag ChIP-seq to analyze the genome-wide binding sites of the endogenous AKAP95. The result showed that there were 5656 binding sites of AKAP95 in the genome. Most of the binding sites were located in promoters (59.23%), followed by introns (17.27%) and intergenic regions (12.14%) (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Data 2). The vicinity of AKAP95-binding regions was enriched with DNA-binding motifs of transcription factors NFY, Sp1 and YY1, which are critical for stem cell fate determination and proliferation27–29 (Supplementary Fig. 7a). Since enhancers are usually located in intergenic regions or introns, we checked whether AKAP95 binding sites fall within the reported enhancers in Hela cells30. 408 typical enhancers and 36 super enhancers showed significant enrichment in AKAP95-bound sites (Supplementary Fig. 7b). These data suggest that AKAP95 may have important roles in regulating gene expression.

Compared with control, knockdown of AKAP95 in Hela cells altered expression of 4270 genes (2372 genes down-regulated, 1898 genes up-regulated, Supplementary Fig. 7c, d and Supplementary Data 3). The down-regulated genes were enriched in AKAP95-binding promoters/genes (n=414, P<0.0001, Fig. 4b). Interestingly, a core subset of MLL-AF9 targets19 (n=177) were also enriched in AKAP95 binding promoters/genes (n=56, P<0.0001), and had significantly higher AKAP95 binding intensity than the rest promoters/genes, suggesting AKAP95 may contribute to MLL-AF9 activated transcription (Fig. 4c, d). Indeed, the down-regulation degree of the AKAP95 and MLL-AF9 joint targets (n=18) was significantly greater than that of other AKAP95 targets (Fig. 4d, e, g and Supplementary Data 4).

We also checked AKAP95-bound RNAs in Hela cells by CLIP-seq. Totally, we identified 2078 RNA-binding sites, corresponding to 1837 mRNA targets. The top RNA-binding sites were categorized into intron (61.26%), followed by promoter (13.47%) and exon (9.33%) (Supplementary Fig. 7e). A quarter of AKAP95 CLIP-targets also had ChIP-binding at the DNA level (Supplementary Fig. 7f).

RNA-binding and phase separation are required for AKAP95 binding to the genome and regulating transcription
We next sought to dissect how AKAP95 as an RBP might regulate transcription. AKAP95 binds to RNA through its zinc finger (ZF) domains16, and has the property of phase separation (PS)15. To check if these two features play roles in AKAP95 binding to chromatin, we established the Hela Flp-In-Trex cells stably expressing AKAP95 (WT or ZF-mutant or PS-mutant)-GFP fusion protein (Supplementary Fig. 8a). Through the cell fractionation process (Fig. 5a), we compared ZF-, PS-mutant subcellular localization to that of AKAP95-WT. ZF- and PS-mutants were easier to be released into the cytoplasmic fraction (S1) after hypotonic treatment than both exogenous and endogenous AKAP95-WT protein (Fig. 5b), likely due to their reduced chromatin-association in the nucleus. For the nuclear fraction (P1), exogenous and endogenous AKAP95 stayed more in the insoluble fraction (chromatin, P2) than in the soluble fraction (nucleoplasm, S2) in the absence of RNase treatment, but this localization status dramatically inverted after RNase treatment. PS-mutant behaved similarly to AKAP95-WT. But ZF-mutant was not responsive to RNase treatment. Moreover, a short treatment with Actinomycin (for 4h), inhibiting transcription, impaired AKAP95 binding to genomic targets as shown in the ChIP-seq analysis (Supplementary Fig. 8b). These data indicate that RNA-binding property is required for AKAP95 binding to chromatin. To measure the intensity of chromatin-associated AKAP95, we treated the P2 fraction with micrococcal nuclease (MNase) and checked the released (S3) and the leftover (P3) portions. Both exogenous and endogenous AKAP95 WT proteins were gradually released into supernatant fraction in a time-dependent manner, but ZF- and PS-mutants had much higher rates in S3 before the MNase treatment and exhibited minimal release further into S3 following the MNase treatment (Fig. 5c and Supplementary Fig. 8c). These results indicate both RNA binding and phase separation properties are required for efficient binding of AKAP95 to chromatin.

Using a chromosomally integrated luciferase reporter gene HEK293T cell line (G-293T)17, we checked AKAP95 variants function in coactivating gene transcription. The results showed that both ZF- and PS-mutant were impaired in activating luciferase gene expression, most likely at the transcriptional level since the reporter gene has no intron (Supplementary Fig. 8d). Then, we checked the genome-wide transcription in the presence of AKAP95-WT, ZF- and PS-mutant individually. To avoid the endogenous AKAP95 interference, we first depleted endogenous AKAP95 by shRNA in the aforementioned established Hela stable cell lines (Supplementary Fig. 8e). We carried out ChIP-seq analysis for total Pol II (RPB1) and actively elongating Pol II, which is phosphorylated at serine 2 of its C-terminal domain (Ser2P). The result showed more occupancy of total Pol II at the promoters in the ZF- and PS-mutant cells than in the AKAP95-WT cells (Fig. 5d). But the mutant cells showed lower Pol II (Ser2P) binding signals across gene bodies than WT cells (Supplementary Fig. 8f). Precision nuclear run-on and sequencing (Pro-seq) analysis also showed that the on-going transcription rates of AKAP95 targets were reduced in mutant cells than in WT cells (Fig. 5e and Supplementary Fig. 9). The degree of Ser2P signals reduction in AKAP95 target genes was positively correlated with the densities of AKAP95 ChIP-seq reads and the level of mRNA down-regulation in both ZF- and PS-mutant compared to the WT control (Supplementary Fig. 8g, h), suggesting that the stronger a target gene is bound by AKAP95, the more reliant it is on both the RNA binding and phase separation properties of AKAP95 for the active transcription of this target gene. These combined data indicate that RNA-binding and phase separation are required for the activity of AKAP95 in driving active transcription.

Previously, we reported that AKAP95 co-immunoprecipitated with Pol II (RPB1) in cells and partially colocalized with Pol II Ser2P15,16. By immunofluorescence staining, we found that ZF-mutant formed discrete foci but hardly overlapped with Pol II Ser2P, and PS-mutant was largely diffusive in the nucleus (Fig. 5f). We purified recombinant AKAP95 and Pol II CTD (aa1356-1767, including 23 heptapeptide repeats) and confirmed AKAP95 directly bound to Pol II CTD by in vitro Pull-down (Supplementary Fig. 10a, b). Consistent with the in vivo phase separation pattern, AKAP95 PS-mutant had poorer phase separation in vitro compared with WT protein (Supplementary Fig. 10c). AKAP95 ZF-mutant had a similar phase separation property as WT protein in the absence of RNA. When RNA was added, the size of AKAP95-WT condensates significantly increased, but the size of ZF-mutant condensates remained unchanged (Supplementary Fig. 10d).

Next, we investigated how AKAP95 phase separation augments Pol II CTD condensation. AKAP95 WT protein underwent co-condensation with Pol II CTD in vitro. Like the single proteins’ behavior, co-condensation of AKAP95 PS-mutant and Pol II CTD was weaker than the WT counterpart (Supplementary Fig. 10e). Importantly, addition of RNA enhanced Pol II CTD recruitment into the condensates, as the size of the droplets was increased. However, the size of the droplets formed by AKAP95 ZF-mutant and Pol II CTD was unaffected by the addition of RNA (Fig. 5g). Taken together, our data suggest that phase separation of AKAP95 augments the co-condensation of Pol II CTD. This mechanism may promote further transcription through recruitment of AKAP95 (and Pol II) mediated by nascent transcripts.

Targeting phase separation of AKAP95 attenuates its chromatin binding and pro-oncogenic function
Consistent with the importance of RNA-binding and phase separation for AKAP95 biochemical functions, we found that these two properties were also essential for cancer cell proliferation. AKAP95 WT, but not the ZF- and PS-mutants, were able to rescue the growth defect of MLLr leukemia cells (THP1 and Molm13) caused by the knockdown of endogenous AKAP95 (Fig. 6a and Supplementary Fig. 11a, b). Immunofluorescence staining showed that MLL1 N-terminal fragments (including MLL1T and WT MLL1 breakage N-terminal part) partially colocalized with AKAP95 WT, but not ZF- and PS-mutants in rescued THP1 cells (Fig. 6b). Meanwhile, we carried out ChIP-seq analysis of the exogenous AKAP95 in the rescued THP1 cells. AKAP95 WT had 916 binding sites on the genomic DNA, but the binding intensity of ZF- or PS-mutant was basically abolished at those sites (Supplementary Fig. 11c). The majority of the AKAP95 binding sites (87.76%) were located in gene promoter regions (Supplementary Fig. 11d and Supplementary Data 5). We noticed a significant enrichment of MLL-AF9 targets in the AKAP95 bound promoters/genes (P=0.0017, Supplementary Fig. 11e). AKAP95 binding intensity at MLL-AF9 target sites was higher than that at the rest sites (the difference was not significant, Supplementary Fig. 11f). This data was similar to the ChIP result of endogenous AKAP95 in Hela cells (Fig. 4d).

Since AKAP95 PS-mutant failed to rescue cell growth defect, we sought to target AKAP95 phase separation to inhibit AKAP95-dependent cancer growth. Heat-shock protein HSP70 changed the composition and fluidity of condensates31,32. Recently, HSP70 cofactor HSP40 (J-domain protein) has been repurposed to dissolve intracellular condensates. Here, we tested whether docking AKAP95 to HSP70 system could abolish AKAP95 phase separation, reduce its binding to chromatin, and attenuate its transcription and pro-oncogenic function.

Because AKAP95 is largely disordered and there is no pocket for designing a small molecule, we designed a 30 aa peptide (PI95) based on the conserved region between PKA RIIa and DPY3017, two interacting proteins of AKAP95 (Supplementary Fig. 12a). We purified GST-AKAP95 and mcherry-PI95 as recombinant proteins and confirmed their binding through co-immunoprecipitation (Supplementary Fig. 12b, c). However, a scrambled version of PI95 (PI95 Scr) failed to bind to AKAP95 (Supplementary Fig. 12d). Flag-HA-mcherry-PI95 was also co-immunoprecipitated with Myc-AKAP95 when these two proteins were both overexpressed in 293T cells (Fig. 6c). These results confirmed that PI95 bound to AKAP95 in vitro and in vivo.

Then, we fused PI95 with a conserved J domain (JD, 1–76 aa) of HSP40, which facilitates HSP70 substrate loading and ATP catalysis33. As the control, we used the H32Q mutant, which failed to interact with HSP7034. Immunoprecipitation of AKAP95 showed that HSP70 was hooked to AKAP95 in the presence of JD-PI95 but not H32Q-PI95 (Supplementary Fig. 12e).

Transduction of Hela cells with lentiviral vector expressing exogenous proteins showed that endogenous AKAP95 protein level was unaffected by the presence of either JD-PI95, H32Q-PI95 or JD-PI95 Scr (Supplementary Fig. 12f). However, AKAP95 dissociated from chromatin faster after MNase treatment in the presence of JD-PI95, but not H32Q-PI95 nor JD-PI95 Scr (Fig. 6d). In LacO-U2OS cells, AKAP95-LacI formed puncta with significantly reduced size at the LacO site when JD-PI95 were overexpressed compared with control or overexpression of H32Q-PI95 or JD-PI95 Scr (Fig. 6e). These data indicate that JD-PI95 impaired AKAP95 phase separation.

Using a double luciferase reporter assay, we checked if JD-PI95 impairs AKAP95’s function in activating transcription. Co-transfected G-293T cells showed significantly reduced luciferase signals in the presence of JD-PI95 (Fig. 6f and Supplementary Fig. 12g). When we introduced JD-PI95 into THP1 cells, the transduced cells had remarkably reduced growth rate compared to the control, H32Q-PI95 or JD-PI95 Scr transduced cells in liquid culture (Fig. 6g). We calculated the nuclear concentration of peptide to be approximately 19–38 nM in THP1 cells, which is in the similar range of most small molecular inhibitors (Supplementary Fig. 12h). When the transduced THP1 cells were injected into immunodeficient mice through tail vein, the mice that received JD-PI95 transduced THP1 had significantly less tumor burden than the other three groups (Fig. 6h). qPCR analysis of the transduced cells showed that the static mRNA levels of several MLL-AF9 targets were significantly reduced in JD-PI95 overexpressed (OE) THP1 cells compared to the control (Supplementary Fig. 13a). Pro-seq analysis of JD-PI95 OE THP1 cells showed that there was a huge difference on 916 transcripts between JD-PI95 treated and non-treated cell (Supplementary Fig. 13b). Although the difference of metagene analysis between JD-PI95 and JD-PI95 scr treated cells was not significant, certain MLL-AF9 targets (RUNX2, SMC4, and NEK7) displayed the lowest on-going transcription in JD-PI95 treated cells (Supplementary Fig. 13c). Together, our data suggest that we were able to design a peptide to effectively impair AKAP95 condensation, dampen its transcription-coactivation function, and attenuate its pro-oncogenic activity.

## Methods

Study approval
The collection of patient bone marrow was approved by the Ethics Committee of Xiangya Hospital Central South University, and written consent for the research purpose was obtained.
The housing and transplantation procedure were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at the University of Virginia. Housing and operating NCG mice were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at Hunan University.

Mouse transplantation procedures
The wild type and Akap95−/− C57BL/6 mice were maintained at the Animal Research Facility at the University of Virginia. CD45.1+ mice were purchased from Jackson Lab. The NCG (NOD/ShiLtJGpt-Prkdcem26Cd52Il2rgem26Cd22/Gpt) mice were purchased from GemPharmatech Co., Ltd. (Jiangsu, China). Mice were housed at 21–22 °C, 30–70% humidity, with a 12:12-h dark:light cycle.
For primary transplantation, 8- to 12-week-old Akap95−/− or WT mouse bone marrow was sorted against Lin− cells using Lineage Cell Depletion kit (Mitenyi Biotech, cat. 130-110-470). Then, the cells were spin-infected with pMSCV-IRES-GFP (Addgene #20672), pMSCV-MLL-AF9-IRES-GFP (a gift from Dr. Golam Mohi, the University of Virginia) retrovirus or pMIR-FLAG-MLL-AF9 (Addgene #71444). 106 transduced cells were injected into lethal irradiated (9.5 Gy) recipient mice (8- to 12-week-old) through the tail vein. The recipients were monitored afterwards. Disease progression included lethargy, rough coat, and loss of weight. Special care (such as a soft diet) was given when mice were hunched. If the situation became even worse after one or two days, the hunched mice were euthanized, and the day was set as the last day of their survival.
For secondary transplantation, the bone marrow harvest from the moribund primary recipient was sorted for the LGMP population. Then, 4000 LGMP cells were injected into sublethal irradiated (6 Gy) recipient mice.
For competitive transplantation, 1×106 Akap95−/− or WT CD45.2+ bone marrow cells were mixed with CD45.1+ bone marrow cells at a 1:1 ratio and injected into CD45.1+ lethal irradiated recipient mice. Tail blood was harvested every 4 weeks after transplantation for blood profile analysis. The recipients were euthanized at 16 weeks for analysis of the cell constitution in bone marrow and spleens.
For leukemia cell line transplantation, 1×106 THP-1 cells transduced with the JD-PI95 constructs and pLent-LucV5 (expressing the luciferase gene) were resuspended in 100 μl PBS and injected into the tail vein of 8-week-old NCG mice. Recipient mice were injected with D-luciferin (Beyotime Biotech; 3 mg per 20 g) intraperitoneally and anaesthetized with isoflurane. Luminescent images were taken within 20 min after D-luciferin intake using an IVIS Spectrum bioluminescence and fluorescence scanner (PerkinElmer) at the Analytical Instrumentation Center of Hunan University. The recipient mice were taken for imaging at 4 weeks after transplantation, and repeated imaging every week before they got weak. The moribund mice were euthanized at the end.

Cell culture
Mouse bone marrow cells harvested for primary transplantation were cultured in IMDM medium (Gibco) with 20% FBS, 100 μg/mL Pen/Strep, 50 μg/mL SCF, 50 μg/mL Flt3 ligand, 10 μg/mL mouse IL-6, 50 μg/mL Tpo and 50 μg/mL mouse IL-3 (PeproTech). Transformed mouse bone marrow cells were cultured in IMDM medium (Gibco) with 20% FBS and 100 μg/mL Pen/Strep.
Cell lines 293T, THP1, Molm13, K562, Jurkat, HL60 were kept in our lab. MV411, Monomac6 and Kasumi were gifts from Dr. Francine Garrett-Bakelman (the University of Virginia). Hela Flp-In-Trex and U2OS-LacO cells were gifts from Dr. Todd P. Stukenburg (the University of Virginia). Plat-E cells were a gift from Dr. Golam Mohi (the University of Virginia). The cells are authenticated by STR profiling from the commercial vendor. Blood cancer cells were cultured in RPIM1640 (Gibco) with 10% FBS and 100 μg/mL Pen/Strep. 293T, Hela, plat-E and U2OS cells were cultured in DMEM (Gibco) with 10% FBS and 100 μg/mL Pen/Strep.

Knock-in cell construction
To tag the endogenous AKAP95 with Flag-mEGFP, sgRNA (5’-CCTGGTCCATGTCTTCGACGCGG-3’) targeting the N-terminus of AKAP95 was cloned into pSpCas9(BB)-2A-Puro V2.0 (Addgene #62988). A DNA fragment composed of Flag-mEGFP flanked by 800-bp homology arms was inserted into pUC19 vector as donor plasmid. Hela cells were transfected with both the sgRNA construct and the linearized donor plasmid through lipo3000 (Life Technologies). After 4 days of selection against puromycin, cells were sorted on GFP signals on Bigfoot spectral cell sorter (Thermo Fisher Scientific). About 8000 GFP-positive cells were seeded in 6-well plates. Colonies were individually transferred into 96-well plates and then expanded. Validation of the positive KI clones was carried out by genotyping, western blot and imaging. Oligos used in this study are listed in the Supplementary Table.

Virus production and transfection of cells
Retrovirus pMSCV-MLL-AF9-IRES-GFP, pMIR-FLAG-MLL-AF9 or pMSCV-IRES-GFP were packaged in plat-E cells. Lentivirus pLKO.1-shAKAP95, pCDH-MSCV-HA-JD-PI95-puro, pCDH-MSCV-HA-H32Q-PI95-puro, and pCDH-MSCV-HA-JD-PI95scr-puro were packaged in 293T cells with the envelope plasmids of psPAX2 and pMD2.G. The virus supernatant was concentrated 30-fold by PEG8000 precipitation, then aliquoted and stored at −80 °C.
For blood cells transduction, 1×106 cells were transduced with 200 μL of concentrated virus by spin infection at 1000×g for 1.5 h. For attached cells transduction, cells grown in one well of a 6-well plate were infection with 200 μL of concentrated virus. Ten to twelve hours later, cells were changed with fresh medium. Twenty-four hours after transduction, cells were subjected to selection. Sometimes, double infections were required for blood cells.

Antibodies
Antibodies used include. WB (antibodies were generally 1:2000 diluted): rabbit anti-AKAP95 (Bethyl Laboratories, A301-061A); mouse anti-GAPDH (Millipore MAB374); rabbit anti-MLL1 (NT86) (Bethyl Laboratories, A300-086A); mouse monoclonal anti-FUS (H-6) (Santa cruz, sc-373698); mouse monoclonal anti-flag (Yeasen Biotech, 30503ES); mouse monoclonal anti-GST (Yeasen Biotech, 30901ES); mouse monoclonal anti-HA (Yeasen Biotech, 30704ES); mouse monoclonal anti-His (Yeasen Biotech, 30401ES).
ChIP, IP, and IF (antibodies were generally 1:500 diluted): Mouse anti-flag magnetic beads (Selleck, B26101); rabbit polyclonal anti-Pol II RBP1 (N-20) (Santa cruz, sc-899); rabbit monoclonal anti-Pol II Ser2P (Cell signaling, #13499); rabbit monoclonal anti-H3K4me3 (Millipore 05-745R); rabbit polyclonal anti-H3K27me3 (Millipore 07-449); rabbit polyclonal anti-H3K27Ac (Abcam ab4729); anti-H3K4me1 (Abcam ab8895); rabbit anti-MLL1 (D2M7U, Cell signaling, #14689); Alex Fluor-555 donkey anti-rabbit IgG (Thermo Fisher Scientific, A-31572).
FACS (antibodies were generally 1:1000 diluted): APC-mouse Lin-cocktail (BD, 51-9006309); anti-mouse CD16/32 Fc block (Biolegend, 101301); PE-anti-mouse c-Kit (BD, 553355); PE-Cy7-anti mouse Sca-I (BD, 558162); BV711-anti-mouse Mac-1 (Biolegend, 101241); BV421-anti-mouse Gr-1 (Biolegend, 108433); BV711-anti-mouse CD16/32 (Biolegend, 101337); BV421-anti-mouse CD34 (Biolegend, 152207); APC-anti-mouse B220 (Biolegend, 103211); Percp-Cy5.5-anti-mouse CD3e (Biolegend, 152311); FITC-anti-mouse CD45.2 (Biolegend, 109806); PE-anti-mouse CD45.1 (Biolegend, 110707); BV510-anti-mouse CD45.1 (Biolegend, 110741).

Flow cytometry and cell sorting
Single-cell suspensions were prepared from bone marrow, spleen, or peripheral blood. Red blood cells were removed using ACK lysis buffer.
The following panel of surface markers was used for separating individual population: LSC (GFP+Lin−c-kit+Mac-1+Gr1+); LGMP (c); LSK (Lin−c-kit+Sca-I+); CMP (Lin−c-kit+Sca-I−CD34+CD16/32−); GMP (Lin−c-kit+Sca-I−CD34+CD16/32+); MEP (Lin−c-kit+Sca-I−CD34−CD16/32−).
FACS analysis was performed on LSR Fortessa (Becton Dickinson), and data were analyzed using FlowJo software (TreeStar).
FACS sorting was performed on LSR Aria II (BD). MLL-AF9 transduced BM were sorted for RFP+Lin−c-Kit+ before being used for the CFC assay. For sorting LGMP cells, BM cells from moribund mice were sorted against GFP+Lin−c-Kit+CD34+CD16/32+.

CFC assay
MLL-AF9 transduced Lin− cells were grown in M3234 methyl Cellulose media (Stem cells) supplemented with 10 μg/mL IL-3, 10 μg/mL IL-6 and 20 μg/mL SCF (PeproTech). Colony numbers were counted 7 to 10 days later. One thousand cells were re-plated in the next round, and this process was repeated 4–5 times.

FRAP
For live-cell imaging of the endogenous Flag-mEGFP labeled AKAP95, Hela cells were grown on 35-mm glass-bottom dishes (Nest Biotech). AKAP95 foci were captured on Zeiss LSM980 confocal microscope with the Airyscan detector. FRAP assay was performed as previously described. For other fluorescence imaging, transfected 293T cells or U2OS cells were observed under Zeiss observer Z1 with 63× oil lens.

Cell fractionation
Stable expression of AKAP95 (WT, ZF- or PS-mutant)-GFP Hela cell lines were established in Hela Flp-In-Trex cells following manufacturer’s instructions. To test the peptide effect, Hela KI cells were transduced with pCDH-alone, pCDH-MSCV-HA-JD-PI95-puro, pCDH-MSCV-HA-H32Q-PI95-puro or pCDH-MSCV-HA-JD-PI95scr-puro lentivirus. After selection, 4×107 cells were collected, washed with PBS and resuspended in 1.5 mL of Buffer A (10 mM HEPES [pH 7.9], 10 mM KCl, 1.5 mM MgCl2, 0.34 M sucrose, 10% glycerol, 1 mM DTT, protease inhibitor cocktail, and 0.1% Triton X-100). The cells were incubated on ice for 8 min, and nuclei (fraction P1) were collected by centrifugation at 1300×g, 4 °C for 5 min. The P1 nuclei were washed once in buffer A and resuspended in 1.5 mL of buffer B (3 mM EDTA, 1 mM DTT and protease inhibitor cocktail), and 0.3 mL of the suspension was saved for WB. The rest suspension was divided into two parts, one added RNase (3 μL, 100 μg/mL final) and one not. After incubation on ice for 30 min, the soluble nuclear fraction (S2) and insoluble fraction (P2) were separated by centrifugation at 1700×g, 4 °C for 5 min. The P2 was washed once with buffer B and resuspended in nuclease digestion buffer (10 mM Tris, 10 mM KCl, and 1 mM CaCl2), then divided into 3 portions (0.2 mL each). One portion was immediately centrifuged to separate the chromatin-associated fraction (S3) and insoluble fraction (P3). The other two portions were added 0.4 μL of MNase (4000 U/mL, New England BioLabs). After incubation at 37 °C for 2 or 5 min, the suspension was centrifuged at 1700×g, 4 °C for 5 min to get S3 and P3 fractions. Equivalent portion of supernatants or pellets was denatured with SDS loading buffer and subjected for western blot.

Immunostaining and imaging
Hela Flp-In-Trex AKAP95 (WT, ZF- or PS-mutant)-GFP cells were further subjected to knockdown of endogenous AKAP95 by lentiviral pLKO.1 vector. Cells were grown on the coverslip, fixed with 4% formaldehyde, and permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X-100. For suspension cells, THP1 cells rescued with pCDH-MSCV-AKAP95 (WT, ZF- or PS-mutant)-GFP lentivirus were cytocentrifuged to glass and fixed. Primary and secondary antibodies were diluted at 1:500. Images were taken on a Zeiss LSM980 confocal microscope with the Airyscan detector.

Co-immunoprecipitation assays
293T or Hela cells transfected or transformed with indicated constructs were harvested and lysed in BC300 (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 300 mM KCl, 20% glycerol, 0.2 mM EDTA) with 0.1% NP40, 1 mM DTT, and protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche, 4693159001). Lysates were incubated with the anti-Flag antibody (Selleck) and washed with lysis buffer. Bead-bound proteins were resolved by SDS-PAGE and detected by immunoblotting.

Double luciferase reporter assay
G-293T cells were transfected with pcDNA5-FH-AKAP95, or ZF-/PS-mutant, together with pGal4-VP16 and pRL. To test the JD-PI95 effect, G-293T cells were co-transfected with pcDNA5-FH-AKAP95 and pcDNA5-HA-JD-PI95 or pcDNA5-HA-JD-PI95Scr in the presence of pGal4-VP16 and pRL. Forty-eight hours later, cells were lysed and detected with a double luciferase reporter kit (Promega). Transcription efficiency was present as firefly luciferase signals normalized by Renilla luciferase signals.

Pol II CTD cloning
Pol II RPB1 CTD were cloned with primers (F: 5’-CGCGGATCC cgcaccacgtccaatga-cattg-3’; R: 5’-CGCGTCGAC gggtgaggttgggctgtagctg-3’) and Hela cDNA as template. RT-PCR products were inserted into the pET28a vector to make pET28a-His-mch-Pol II CTD. Several clones were sent to Sanger sequencing. The plasmid harboring aa 1356-1767 (including 23 heptapeptide repeats) was used for protein purification.

Protein purification and in vitro immunoprecipitation
Plasmids pET28a serials or pGEX-AKAP95 were transformed into E. coli BL21 Star (DE3) (Yeasen Biotech). Bacterial culture at OD600 of 0.6 was induced with 0.4 mM of IPTG (Yeasen Biotech) for 5 h at 25 °C. For purification of 6×His-tagged proteins, bacterial pellets from 500 ml IPTG-induced culture were resuspended in 6 mL of lysis buffer 50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.3, 450 mM NaCl, 10 mM imidazole, 1× protease inhibitors (Roche) and lysed by sonication. After centrifugation, the supernatant was incubated with 1 mL of pre-equilibrated HisSep Ni-NTA Resin (Yeasen Biotech, 20502ES) for 1–2 h at 4 °C, washed with wash buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.3, 450 mM NaCl, 20 mM imidazole), and eluted with 0.5 mL elution buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.3, 450 mM NaCl, 250 mM imidazole) 5 times. For purification of GST-tagged proteins, bacterial lysates were incubated with GSTSep Glutathione agarose beads (Yeasen Biotech, 20507ES) and washed 3 times with wash buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.3, 450 mM NaCl). Then, the GST-AKAP95-contained beads were incubated with the His-tagged protein solution at 4 °C for 3 h. After a thorough wash, the beads were resuspended in SDS-loading buffer and subjected to immunoblotting. Purified proteins were also validated by Coomassie blue staining.

Estimation of peptide concentration
By immunoblotting of lysates from a known number of cells along with the purified and quantified Flag-JD-PI95 protein, and based on the nuclear volume of 220 fl of HeLa cells, we calculated the concentration of peptide to be approximately 19–38 nM in THP1 cells.

In vitro phase separation
Image-based phase separation was carried out as previously described. Briefly, purified proteins were stored in high salt concentration and without PEG, and were diluted using a “condensation buffer” into a final condition of indicated protein concentration, 150 mM NaCl and 7.5% PEG8000, 50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.3, 10% glycerol, 1 mM DTT. AKAP95 and Pol II CTD co-condensation was carried out by mixing the two proteins for 1–2 mins then diluting the mixture with condensation buffer. Total Hela cell RNA was added to the protein solution before the condensation buffer. Protein mixtures were added to a homemade flow chamber comprised of a glass slide sandwiched by a coverslip with one layer of double-sided tape as a spacer. Images were taken on a Zeiss Axio Observer Z1 microscope with a 63× oil lens. Fluorescent and differential interference contrast (DIC) microscopy images were taken.

RNA extraction and RNA-seq analysis
RNA extraction was done by the Trizol method. RNA integrity was confirmed by gel electrophoresis. qPCR was carried out with SYBR green and quantified with 2−ΔΔCt method. For RNA-seq library preparation, mRNA was enriched by polyA+ selection, converted to cDNA, labeled with adapters and barcodes with NEBNext Ultra II Directional RNA Library Prep Kit for Illumina (New England BioLabs, E7760). The 75 bp pair-end sequencing was performed using the Next-seq (Illumina).
RNA-seq reads were aligned to the human genome assembly GRCH37/hg19 or the mouse genome assembly GRCm38/mm10 using STAR. RNA-seq counts were annotated using RSEM. Read counts were normalized to TPM (transcripts per million reads). Differentially expressed genes were calculated using DE-seq2. Significant DEGs were selected at the thresholds of adjusted P value < 0.05 and |fold change| > 2 if otherwise described. Gene ontology and pathway analysis were conducted using DAVID v6.8 (https://david.ncifcrf.gov/summary.jsp) and GSEA. Heatmaps of differentiated genes between treatments were plotted with the R package ggplot2.

ChIP and ChIP-seq analysis
ChIP was carried out as previously described with individual antibodies. The immunoprecipitated DNA was used for ChIP-seq library preparation with the NEBNext Ultra II DNA library Prep Kit for Illumina (New England BioLabs, E7645). Libraries were sequenced using the Next-seq sequencer (Illumina) in single-end 75 bp mode.
ChIP-seq reads were aligned to the human genome assembly GRCH37/hg19 or mouse genome assembly GRCm38/mm10 using BWA. Sam files were converted into bam files using Samtools. MACS2 was used to call peaks under the FDR threshold of 0.01. For H3K4me1, 3 and H3K27ac ChIP-seq data, SICER258 was applied to call broad peaks (islands) with default parameters. AKAP95 ChIP-seq peaks were called with MACS software (version 1.4.3). AKAP95 binding sites were annotated with the Homer software as promoter (1.5 kb upstream of transcription start site), 5’ UTR, exon, intron, 3’ UTR, small noncoding RNA, TTS (1 kb downstream of transcription terminal site) and intergenic region.
Hela cell enhancers were referred to previously reported information. ChIP-seq read density in these regions was calculated and plotted with the DeepTools software. For the PolII and Ser2P, each mapped bam file was normalized with the counts per million mapped reads method and plotted with the Deeptools software. Motif enrichment analysis in AKAP95 ChIP-seq was performed using HOMER software to identify the transcription factor characterized by a motif enriched with the most significant P-value. The overlapping peaks between ChIP and CLIP were determined using the MergePeaks function of the HOMER software with an interval distance of 5 kb.

CLIP and CLIP-seq analysis
Cells grown in 10-cm dishes were crosslinked with 600 mJ/cm2 of 254 nm UV light. The nuclei were prepared by incubating cells in hypotonic buffer (10 mM HEPES [pH 7.9], 10 mM KCl, 1.5 mM MgCl2, 0.34 M sucrose, 10% glycerol, 1 mM DTT, protease inhibitor cocktail, 0.1% Triton X-100 and 400 U/mL RNase inhibitor). Isolated nuclei were resuspended in lysis buffer (1X PBS, 0.5% NP-40, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate, 0.1% SDS and 400 U/mL RNase inhibitor). After brief sonication, the lysate was centrifuged at 1300×g, 4 °C for 10 min. The supernatants were incubated with 40 μL pre-equilibrated anti-flag beads (Selleck) at 4 °C overnight. Then, the beads were washed twice with cold CLIP lysis buffer and two more times with high salt wash buffer (5X PBS, 0.5% NP-40, 0.5% sodium deoxycholate, 0.1% SDS and 400 U/mL RNase inhibitor). The protein-RNA complex-bound beads were washed four times with PNK buffer (50 mM Tris pH 7.4, 10 mM MgCl2, 0.5% NP-40). The RNAs were partially digested with MNase (New England BioLabs, 1:105 diluted) at 37 °C for 10 min. The reaction was stopped by PNK-EGTA buffer (PNK buffer with 2 mM EGTA). Then the beads were washed twice with PNK buffer. To dephosphorylate the RNA, the beads were treated with CIP (New England BioLabs) for 10 min at 37 °C. After two more washes with PNK buffer, the pre-adenylated 3’ linker (rAppCTGTAGGCACCATCAAT-NH2, Beyotime Biotech, R0700S) was ligated with truncated T4 RNA ligase 2 (New England BioLabs) at 16 °C overnight. Then the non-ligated 3’ linker was washed away with two washes of CLIP lysis buffer and two washes of PNK buffer. The RNAs were then phosphorylated by T4 PNK (New England BioLabs) for 10 min at 37 °C. To elute the protein-RNA complex, the samples were treated with Proteinase K (50 mM Tris, pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 0.5% SDS, and 20 mg Proteinase K) for 30 min at 37 °C. The RNAs were purified and ligated with 5’ RNA adapter (GUUCAGAGUUCUACAGUCCGAC, Sangon Biotech) by T4 RNA ligase (New England BioLabs). Then the RNAs were reverse transcribed by Superscript III (Life Technologies) with RT primer (CTGTAGGCACCATCAAT, Sangon Biotech) and amplified for 20 cycles with Q5 DNA polymerase (New England BioLabs) (Primer_Forward: GTTCAGAGTTCTACAGTCCGAC; Primer_Reverse: CTGTAGGCACCATCAAT, Sangon Biotech). Library index sequence was introduced by PCR with index primers (Forward (SR primer): AATGATACGGCGACCACCGAGATCTACACGTTCAGAGTTCTACAGTC CGAC, Reverse: CAAGCAGAAGACGGCATACGAGATCGTGATGTGACT GGAGTTC CTGTAGGCACCATCAAT) (the underlined hexamer indicates Illumina index sequence, Sangon Biotech) for eight more cycles.
AKAP95 binding sites were annotated as promoter (1 kb upstream of transcription start site), 5’ UTR, exon, intron, 3’ UTR, small noncoding RNA, TTS (1 kb downstream of transcription terminal site) and intergenic region. Alternative splicing isoforms were analysed as previously described with MISO software with its version 2.0 annotation of all known alternative splicing events according to the online documentation https://miso.readthedocs.io/en/fastmiso/.

Pro-seq signaling
Pro-seq library construction was performed as previously described. Libraries were sequenced using the Next-seq sequencer (Illumina) in single-end 75 bp mode.
Sequence reads were aligned to the human genome assembly GRCH37/hg19 using BWA. Sam files were converted into bam files using Samtools55. MACS2 was used to call peaks under the FDR threshold of 0.01. To generate the coverage of the aligned sequence reads, the bam files were converted to BEDPE files using BEDtools. Only the 5′ end of mate 1 reads were kept into a bed file and converted into bedGraph files using “bedtools genomecov -bg –strand”. The raw read counts in bigWig coverage tracks were normalized by sequencing depth (counts per million mapped reads). The Pro-seq metagene plot was generated with the deeptools software.

Statistics
Experimental data are presented as the mean ± s.d. of three independent experiments unless otherwise noted. Statistical analysis was carried out by two-sided unpaired Student’s t test (for two-sample comparison), log-rank test (for survival analysis), or Fisher’s exact test (for gene overlap), Mann–Whitney U Test (for omics analysis) as indicated in figure legends. Statistical analysis was performed using Prism, Excel or Python. A P value of less than 0.05 was considered significant. Statistical significance levels if otherwise described are denoted as follows: *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001 and ****P < 0.0001.

In this paper, the authors studied the function of AKAP95, an established RNA binding protein (RBP) and transcriptional
cofactor, in regulating oncogenic effects of MLL-fusion (MLLr) proteins in AML. First, authors reported that AKAP95 is over-
expressed in MLL-r AML and AKAP95 loss slowed the proliferation of MLLr AML in vitro and in vivo. Authors also used
RNA-seq, ChIP-seq and CLIP-seq to show that AKAP95 associates with both target genes and target transcripts to
modulate the transcriptional levels. Using the cell fractionation and cell imaging experiments, authors further demonstrated
that AKAP95 relies on the RNA binding functon(within a zinc finger domain) and phase separation functon(within IDR; PS
mutation of Tyr to Ser in aa 101-210) to tightly bind onto chromatin targets. Interestingly, PS mutant failed to phase separate
and also failed to interact with MLL1-T and had a weaker co-condensation with RNA POL II CTD. Lastly, authors proposed
to use heat shock protein to disrupt phase separation property of AKAP95; and on this line, they used a JD-PI95 fusion to
treat MLLr AML. Preliminary data showed the effects of JD-PI95 in vitro and in vivo. Overall, this work presented interesting
findings and studied a potentially important phenomenon related to phase separation, gene regulation and leukemia
development. But some shown datasets were not carefully analyzed. Writing requires extensive editing. I have a few
comments as listed below.
Main comments.
(1) This work used RNA-seq to define the differentially expressed genes after AKAP95 loss. But whether these genes are
upregulated or downregulated is not specified. This refers to Figure 3 such as 3B and 3C. Authors seem to suggest
downregulation in Fig 3C? The detected changes need to be verified with other methods such as qPCR.

### Reviewer 2

The manuscript by Yan and colleagues studies the potential role of AKAP95 (aka AKAP8) in transcriptional control. The
investigators use a combination of genetics and genomics to make the argument that AKAP95 is not only critical for MLL
fusion protein action, but also for RNA polymerase functions through inducing condensate formation. The authors have
generated a lot of data that indicates that AKAP95 is not required for normal cellular functions or for hematopoietic stem and
progenitor cell function, even in the face of a bone marrow transplant. These results suggest that AKAP95 is not required for
the majority of transcriptional control, even under stress conditions when cells must rapidly cycle to replenish the bone
marrow. Nevertheless, when comparing cells with or without AKAP95, there were changes in about 5% of the transcripts,
which likely describes the change in cell phenotype.
The challenge in trying to establish that an RNA binding protein is regulating transcription is determining whether the
“chicken or the egg” comes first. That is, is RNA polymerase regulating AKAP95 condensate formation by making a nascent
RNA that recruits AKAP95 to chromatin or is AKAP95 regulating transcription by binding to DNA or to RNA Polymerase?
Unfortunately, the genetic approaches employed are too slow to establish cause and effect relationships, as even the
shRNAs take a couple of days to inhibit AKAP95. However, the investigators have a system in which they could integrate a
degron tag into the endogenous alleles of AKAP95, which would allow rapid degradation of AKAP95. A short time course of
degradation (0, 15’, 30’, 60’) coupled with PRO-seq would define the changes in nascent transcription and determine if
AKAP95 is required for transcription initiation and/or elongation. Without a doubt, this would be a lot of work, but it is
necessary to prove the conclusions that the authors are trying to make. Currently, the work suggests that AKAP95 is not
critical for RNA polymerase functions, but might contribute to the fine tuning of some genes, perhaps even some that are
important for MLL fusion protein action.
Major Comments:
1) The work relies heavily on shRNA knockdowns that trigger inflammation and have other off target effects. It would be
useful to confirm the key findings using CRISPRs and to compare the data with those in the DEPMAP.
2) ChIP-seq data are not convincing as shown. The scales on the IGV screen shots are very small, which implies very low
signal over the noise. This should be benchmarked to the signal of RNA Pol II to give the reader a comparison. It really looks
like AKAP95 just binds nascent RNA, and it is getting crosslinked to DNA via its recruitment by RNA or through RNA
polymerase. That is, transcription is regulating AKAP95 rather than AKAP95 regulating transcription. This could be tested by
degrading RNA polymerase using a short treatment with  -amanintin prior to ChIP-seq analysis, which would establish that
AKAP95 binds to the promoters identified.
3) If one accepts the ChIP-seq data, then only 29 genes showed both differential regulation, ChIP signal and CLIP signal,
yet all RNA Pol II was affected by the expression of the mutants (Fig. 5E). It seems likely that this is just due to the cells
growing more slowly (i.e., sick cells) rather than an interaction with chromatin.
4) The genomic analysis in Figures 3-4 don’t hold together well. If AKAP95 is at 3348 promoters (roughly 1/3 of the
expressed genes), why are so few genes affected by knockout of the gene? The most common artifact of ChIP-Seq is a
small signal at promoters, but if the signal is real, why is there no effect on H3K4me3 levels at MLL fusion protein targets
(Fig. 3E)? Moreover, there were large changes in H3K27ac genome wide (Fig. 3D), which implies that all genes were
repressed to some degree?
5) The PRO-seq data indicates no effect of AKAP95 on nascent transcription, but it is a very unusual plot in that there is as
much antisense transcription as sense and there is little divergence between the WT and the mutants. The histograms
shown are also quite confusing in that they show both sense and antisense transcription at -1000 bp from the TSS. The
authors should consider showing some screen shots that show a possible defect in nascent transcription more clearly.
6) If the fusion peptide truly inhibits condensate formation, then treating cells with the peptide and performing a short time
course (0, 15’, 30’, 60’) of PRO-seq should define the role of AKAP95 in transcription control. It would be expected to cause
a collapse of RNA polymerase at AKAP95-regulated loci.
Minor:
1) The authors might want to consider breaking the work into two manuscripts. The MLL story doesn’t really integrate well
with the HeLa and 293 cell work, as the is presumably not much overlap in regulated genes. There is a lot of data here, but it
doesn’t fit together in a very coherent manner.
2) The motif analysis doesn’t add anything to the story, as these are just binding sites associated with promoters.
3) It would probably be prudent to avoid calling myeloid progenitor cells LSCs unless formally proven to be LSC through
limiting dilution analysis.
